title: Trumpet endurance, laying off, and spontaneous jazz
summary: Edison says he dislikes practising, and compares jazz spontaneity to studio work.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Also, with a trumpet player there is the sort of endurance, which is different for a saxophone player, really, isn't it?
Right. It's much different. See, a saxophone player don't need any teeth to play.
Just has to keep these muscles up.

Just has to keep his muscles right there, see. But a trumpet player, man, he can lay off his horn for days and come back, you know. Only thing he looses is he's got to get his fingers together. But when you lay off of a trumpet, you have one little spot that you can play there.
What do you do when you lay off for a couple of weeks or so? Do you pick it up?
I just have to hope and pray, when I do play I can get a sound out. Because I don't like to practice.

I just have to hope that, well, when we do start -- but playing jazz is a lot different than playing in the studios, you know. You can -- jazz is spontaneous. You're supposed to make mistakes playing jazz, you know.
Yes, I was going to say, to begin with you can sort of fake.

Yeah, until you build yourself up, you know. You have to go back in your old trick bag and use some of the wisdom that you have acquired all through the years, you know, to supplement. What a youngster would do is just get up there and try to blow right now.
